items.source: Education Week / Stanford AI Hub for Education
items.title: 52 real tests out of 1,686 papers: what the evidence on AI and learning says
items.explainer: Stanford's AI Hub for Education reviewed the 52 randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies in its repository of 1,686 papers on AI in education. A randomized trial assigns students to use a tool or not by chance, so differences in learning can be traced to the tool. Across the 52, students who used AI for support, such as explanations or practice problems, generally learned more than students who used it to complete their work, though neither use was consistently positive.
items.why: It gives a teacher one evidence-backed rule for designing AI use: point the tool at practice and explanation, not at producing the graded work.

items.title: LLMON: a markup language built into the model to separate instructions from data
items.explainer: IBM released preview Granite 4.1 models (3B and 8B) trained on LLMON, a markup format whose six structural delimiters are reserved special tokens that never appear in ordinary text. Every block of instructions, data or requirements gets an ID, and an exec block says which instructions apply to which data, much like passing arguments to a function. IBM reports it resists prompt injection, where text inside a document hijacks the model, far better than plain prompts, though these are IBM's own benchmarks on experimental models.
items.why: Any AI tool that reads student work, email or web pages can be steered by hidden text in that content, and this is the first serious attempt to fix it inside the model rather than in the prompt.

items.title: AI is getting weird again
items.explainer: Potkalitsky argues that the open question about AI has shifted from what the systems are to whether they can speed up their own development, a process called recursive self-improvement. He points to an Anthropic report saying Claude wrote more than 80% of the code merged into its production codebase by May 2026, while Pew polling shows public concern stuck at 52% since 2023. His point is that insiders may notice a change well before the public or schools do.
items.why: It is a clear, sourced way to explain to faculty why AI guidance written a year ago may already be out of date.

tryThisWeek.title: Move one AI task from doing to practicing
tryThisWeek.steps: Pick one assignment where students now use AI to produce part of the work. Rewrite the AI step so the tool only explains a concept or generates five practice items, and students write the graded piece themselves. Ask them afterward which version helped them remember more.

hook: Out of 1,686 research papers on AI in education, how many actually tested whether an AI tool helped students learn?

lead.title: Thousands of papers, a handful of tests
lead.dek: A Stanford review finds that only 52 of 1,686 papers on AI in education tested whether a specific use changed learning, and the answer depends on how students used it.
paragraphs: Stanford's AI Hub for Education keeps a repository of research on generative AI in schools and colleges. Of the 1,686 papers in it, only 52 tested the impact of a specific intervention, using randomized controlled trials or quasi-experimental designs. The Hub's new review of those 52, reported by Education Week on Nov. 10, updates a similar review from March. Only 10 of the 52 were done with U.S. K-12 students or educators.

The clearest pattern is about use, not tools. When students used generative AI for learning support, such as explanations of concepts or practice problems, learning gains were generally better than when they used it to complete their work. Neither use produced consistent positive results across studies. Teacher use could raise the quantity and quality of feedback, though at least one study found it lowered student motivation and confidence.

The thin base is also a quality problem. In a separate Education Week story on Nov. 2, Patrick O'Neill of Ivy Tech Community College described his audit of 14 meta-analyses, drawn from nearly 40 that concluded AI improves learning; all 14 failed basic research standards, such as pooling different populations and measures. Those papers have been cited more than 3,000 times, and one in Nature was retracted a year after it appeared. Susanna Loeb, a Stanford education professor and an author of the review, put it plainly: "There is plenty of evidence that unless carefully used, these tools can reduce learning."
lead.against: Fifty-two rigorous studies in under four years is fast for education research, and the support-versus-completion pattern matches decades of learning science on practice and explanation. Waiting for a complete evidence base means teachers decide with no evidence at all.
lead.watch: Whether the Hub's next update adds more U.S. classroom trials, and whether AI vendors start publishing controlled studies instead of usage counts.
lead.ask: In your ESL and LENS classes, which AI uses are support and which are completion, and which one could you move to the support side this week?

graph.title: A big pile of research, a small stack of tests
graph.tease: Stanford's AI Hub for Education collects research on generative AI in teaching and learning. Its November update draws on a repository of 1,686 papers, up from more than 800 studies in its earlier 2026 review.
graph.question: How many of the 1,686 papers actually tested whether a specific AI use changed learning?

panels.label: Papers and studies the reviews drew on
Studies with a strong test of whether AI changed learning

graph.reveal: Just 52 of 1,686, about 3 percent, and the earlier review found 20 out of more than 800. When someone cites the research on AI and learning, ask how many studies actually tested the thing.
graph.caveat: Counts as reported by Education Week on Nov. 2 and Nov. 10, 2026; the reviews themselves were not read at the source. The earlier figure is a floor (more than 800), and each review used its own inclusion rules.

argue.claim: A school that adopts AI because it feels inevitable has already let the vendor set its teaching priorities.
argue.context: Audrey Watters argues that resistance to AI is real and growing, that ed-tech has long embedded its backers' priorities in schools, and that institutions should put people rather than machines at their center.
